connector: Here’s a question before we open the book: what if every time someone else broke a rule, you got in trouble for it? In today’s chapters you’ll meet a boy whose whole job is exactly that. Watch who gives the orders, who gets punished, and how each boy feels about it.

plate.credit: Les Très Riches Heures du Duc de Berry, January (detail) · Limbourg brothers, 1412–1416 · Public domain
plate.look: A duke’s New Year feast, painted by hand in a book more than 600 years ago. Lords in fine clothes crowd around a long table full of food. Chapter 1 opens at a grand feast like this one.

mfill1.h1: Say the two parts out loud, one right after the other.
mfill1.why: the part that means between, plus rupt (break): to break in between.

mfill2.h1: Put the first part in front of a word you already know.
mfill2.why: the part that means between, plus act: to act between people.

mfill3.h1: The second part is a whole word. Just stick the first part on the front.
mfill3.why: the part that means between, plus national: between nations.

mfill4.h1: The second part has to do with the sea. Join them with no space.
mfill4.why: the part that means under, plus marine (sea): a boat that goes under the sea.

match.exasperation: Exasperation is a feeling that builds and builds. Look for the meaning about frustration.
match.contrite: Contrite is how someone looks when they are truly sorry. Look for the meaning about feeling ashamed.
match.forbidden: Forbidden is about rules. Look for the meaning that says something is not allowed.
match.defiantly: Defiantly tells how someone does something: boldly, refusing to obey. Look for that one.

cards.title: Why a Whipping Boy?
cards.sub: A real prince, and the rule in this book
cards.look: A painting of a real English prince named Edward. It was painted about 500 years ago, when he was about one year old. The words at the bottom are in Latin, an old language.

art.alt: A painting of a baby prince in a red and gold outfit and a feathered hat
art.title: Edward VI as a Child
art.creator: Hans Holbein the Younger

text: In this book, nobody is allowed to spank a prince. So the king keeps a boy from the streets in the castle, to be punished in the prince’s place. That boy is called the whipping boy.
Stories say Prince Edward had a friend who took his punishments. Nobody knows for sure if that is true. In The Whipping Boy, it is the rule, and Jemmy is the boy who pays for it.

cards.title: Jemmy’s Street Talk
cards.sub: How Jemmy talks, in everyday words
cards.look: Jemmy grew up on the city streets long ago, and he talks the way people there talked. The author wrote it that way on purpose, so you can hear Jemmy’s voice. It is not a mistake in the book.
cards.todo: Tap each thing Jemmy says to see it in everyday words.
cards.finish: Now you can hear Jemmy’s voice when you read.

transcripts.welcome: Hello again, it’s Opti. Today we open a brand-new book, The Whipping Boy. Here’s something to think about: what if you got in trouble every time someone else broke a rule? Hold on to that question. First you’ll warm up your words, then you’ll read the first two chapters, and at the end you’ll decide what you think of the prince.
transcripts.guide1: Before the word work, here’s a little secret. Long words are often built from smaller pieces, the way a castle is built from stones. Today you’ll find two of those pieces and figure out what each one means, before the page tells you. After that come some joining words and some vowel pairs. Take it one step at a time.
transcripts.guide2: Before you open the book: Chapter 1 has a feast, a prank, and a boy in a cold tower. As you read, keep asking yourself who gives the orders, and who has to obey. And listen to how Jemmy talks. He grew up on the city streets, and the author wants you to hear it.
transcripts.guide3: Now it’s your turn to have an opinion. A good claim names a character, says what you think of them, and hints at why. You can pick any character, as long as the book gives you a reason. Think back over the feast and the lessons. Then write your claim in one strong sentence.
transcripts.card-whip: This little prince was real. His name was Edward, and he lived in England about five hundred years ago. Stories say a friend of his took his punishments, but nobody knows if that’s true. In our book, it’s the rule, and Jemmy is the one who pays.
transcripts.card-street: Jemmy talks like the streets he grew up on. Words like ain’t and me rags aren’t mistakes. The author wrote them on purpose so you can hear Jemmy in your head. Tap each one to find out what it means.

notes.wgrd: Good readers notice who has power at the start of a story: who gives the orders, and who has to obey.
vocab: a strong feeling of frustration that has been building up
feeling truly sorry and ashamed for something you did wrong
done in a bold, refusing-to-obey way
notes.wordParts: inter- means “between” (interrupt, interact, international). sub- means “under” (submarine).
notes.grammar: A conjunction is a joining word. and adds an idea, but shows a difference, and so shows a result.
notes.spelling: A vowel team is two vowels that make one sound, like ai in rain. A team stays together in one syllable: rain·bow, sea·son.
